stories.brief: On her usual walk to the bus stop, Dana notices that a raised paving stone is difficult to see and could trip someone. She asks a municipal service representative how to report the spot and explains exactly where it is, using a nearby shop as a landmark. The representative asks whether the stone is loose or simply uneven; Dana clarifies that one edge moves when stepped on. She asks what details are useful and whether she can attach a photograph, then repeats the instructions to make sure she understood. Dana sends the location and photo through the indicated reporting channel, notes the reference information, and warns a neighbor to watch their step while awaiting an update.

Friends Ravit and Oren sign up for a guided birdwatching morning at a nearby nature area because Oren has borrowed binoculars and Ravit wants to learn how to use them. At the meeting point, the guide asks what they hope to see; Ravit says she would rather learn to notice ordinary birds than chase a rare sighting. When Oren realizes the binocular strap is tangled, the guide shows him how to adjust it and explains how to focus without startling the birds. They walk quietly along the marked path, stop to compare a bird’s call with its appearance, and ask the guide how to tell two similar birds apart. They identify one together, jot down its name, and leave with a short list of places to look for birds on their next local walk.

stories.brief: Freelancer Noga receives a tax notice she does not understand and brings it to her accountant rather than guessing what it means. She points to a section that seems to refer to information missing from her file and asks the accountant to explain the wording. The accountant says they should check the notice against her records before drawing conclusions; Noga admits that she has not yet gathered all the relevant receipts. They identify which documents may help clarify the notice, and Noga asks where to find the applicable instructions and whether any response is needed. The accountant agrees to review the notice and records, then send her the relevant official instructions and a written summary of the next steps. Noga makes a list of the documents to collect and sets a time to follow up, without assuming a deadline or amount that has not been confirmed.

Yael explains the change and asks what options are available; Tomer clarifies that another authorized adult can collect him, but asks Yael to confirm who she has in mind. She suggests her sister, then checks what information the coordinator needs and whether the sister should call or speak to staff at the entrance. stories.brief: A collection of independent short practical situations from ordinary daily life.

shortItems.brief: A customer asks a bank representative whether a transfer marked pending has gone through. The representative suggests checking the transaction details, and the customer finds the transfer is still processing.

A patient calls a clinic to ask whether to bring anything to an appointment. The receptionist suggests checking the appointment message, where the patient finds a note to bring a list of current medicines.

A person calling a health service asks how to explain a new skin irritation clearly. The staff member suggests noting when it appeared and where it is, so the caller writes those details down before speaking with a clinician.
A customer points to an unclear line on a medicine label and asks the pharmacist what it means. The pharmacist explains the wording and recommends following the label rather than guessing.
A tenant notices a loose kitchen cabinet handle and asks the landlord where to send a photo. The landlord gives a preferred contact method, and the tenant sends the picture with a short description.
At a supermarket counter, a shopper asks another customer whether they are waiting in line. The customer says yes and points out where the line begins, so the shopper takes their place behind them.
A customer starting an online return asks a friend where to find the printable return label. The friend points to the order page, and the customer downloads the label to print it.

A driver parked in an unfamiliar area asks a nearby attendant where to check the parking instructions. The attendant points to a sign with a code, and the driver scans it to review the options before paying.

Before entering a small concert, a visitor cannot find the ticket confirmation on their phone and asks a friend for help. The friend suggests searching the email inbox for the event name, and the visitor finds the message.
While helping prepare dinner, a guest asks which spoon to use to taste the sauce. The cook hands over a clean teaspoon, and the guest tastes it and says it needs a little more salt.
A visitor at a riverside park asks a guide where the marked walking path begins. The guide points to a wooden sign beside the bridge, and the visitor starts along the marked route.

stories.brief: Baruch Agadati organized Tel Aviv’s first Queen Esther beauty pageant for a 1926 Purim ball; Lyla Tchertkov won although she had not formally entered, and the contest became a local Purim tradition.

sources.title: Meet Queen Esther – Israel’s First Beauty Queen
“Our Only Romantic Festival”: Hebrew Queen Esther

storyBeats: In 1926, Tel Aviv artist and dance producer Baruch Agadati added a Queen Esther election to his Purim masquerade ball, linking the holiday’s biblical heroine with the young Hebrew city’s public festivities.
The first Queen Esther, Lyla Tchertkov, had come to the ball as a guest and had not formally entered the contest; the audience chose her there.
A contemporary account described Tchertkov as having green eyes and black hair; her appearance became part of the press coverage of the new contest.
The Queen Esther was not only a ball title: the selected woman could lead Tel Aviv’s Purim street procession, riding in an open car with Agadati.
The queen was chosen at a special gala, generally held about a month before Purim, by people who bought tickets to the event.
Instead of a cash award, the winner received a large vase or another decorative household object.
The event drew objections from religious critics who regarded beauty contests as indecent and foreign, and from intellectuals who argued that the spectacle undermined Hebrew society’s morals.

A 1926 letter to the newspaper Davar objected to selecting a queen by popular vote, arguing that beauty should not be elected and that donating part of the ball’s proceeds to the Jewish National Fund did not make the contest acceptable.
Agadati publicly defended continuing the contest after the criticism, describing the first election as a prelude to future Purim balls.
The election helped inspire other Purim balls in Palestine to choose their own Queen Esther or beauty queen; Agadati’s contest was discontinued amid public pressure around 1930.

stories.brief: A National Library investigation identified Ahuva Naftali-Yoktan as the likely baby in a 1948 photograph series catalogued as “The State of Israel’s First Baby”; she was born in Jerusalem shortly after the state was declared.

sources.title: Revealed: Who Was “The State of Israel’s First Baby”?
חשיפה: מי את ״תינוקת ראשונה במדינת ישראל״?

storyBeats: A series of 1948 photographs in the National Library of Israel was catalogued under the title “The State of Israel’s First Baby,” but the catalog initially gave no name or location for the infant.

The photographs show the same infant in the arms of hospital nurses; they were taken by photographer Benno Rothenberg and are held in the Meitar Collection of the Pritzker Family National Photography Collection.
The National Library researcher found the images while looking through the catalog and checked Rothenberg’s original logbooks, but the logbooks did not identify the baby either.
A lead came from journalist Maya Ronen’s 2023 Davar article about people who shared their birthday with Israel’s declaration; one interviewee, Hannah Goren, helped the researcher make new contacts.
The Library’s investigation identified Ahuva Naftali-Yoktan as the likely baby in the photographs, while describing the identification as highly likely rather than absolutely certain.
Ahuva was born on May 14, 1948, at 4:45 p.m. at Hadassah Hospital, then located on HaNevi’im Street in Jerusalem, shortly after Israel’s declaration of independence.
The photographs’ nurses wore pins that researchers identified as belonging to nurses from the Hadassah School of Nursing, supporting the connection to that hospital.
Ahuva recalled that Jerusalem was under blockade and that her mother walked to the hospital while in labor because there was no other way to get there.

Ahuva said that six boys and one girl were born in Jerusalem that day, a reminder that the phrase “first baby” in the photograph’s title does not establish that she was the first child born anywhere in the new state.

As a child, Ahuva joined events for people born on Israel’s declaration day, including a special Jerusalem Municipality trip when she was nine and a later torch-lighting ceremony with other birthday celebrants.

translations.en: on the day of the declaration of independence

stories.brief: Producer Zvi Spielmann and partner Alex Massis founded Israfilm in 1965; the company helped produce Israeli features and the early films of directors including Moshe Mizrahi and Judd Neeman.
storyBeats: Zvi Spielmann entered the Israeli film industry in 1952, joining Herzliya Studios after Margot Klausner invited him; he worked across production roles before founding Israfilm.
In 1965, Spielmann and Alex Massis founded Israfilm as a motion-picture production company; producer Shlomo Morgabi later joined them.
Israfilm specialized in co-productions and also provided production services to foreign companies filming partly or wholly in Israel.
Its work included Israeli-based production services for Bloomfield, also known as The Hero, in 1970, and for Steven Spielberg’s Schindler’s List in 1993.
Israfilm co-produced international projects including A Woman Called Golda, starring Ingrid Bergman, and Remembrance of Love, starring Kirk Douglas.
Other listed international co-productions include The Little Drummer Girl, with Diane Keaton, and Sword of Gideon, with Steven Bauer, Rod Steiger, and Michael York.
Israfilm backed feature debuts by young Israeli directors, including Judd Neeman’s The Dress (1969) and Moshe Mizrahi’s The Customer of the Off Season (1970).
The archive credits Israfilm with The Dress, a 75-minute feature directed by Neeman, and Requiem for a Fish, a 14-minute short directed by Joseph Rimmer, in 1968.
The company’s Israeli credits span different forms and subjects, from the 1989 feature One of Us to the 1972 documentary Ben-Gurion Remembers.
The Zvi Spielmann and Family Israfilm Collection was entrusted to the Israel Film Archive, which maintains, preserves, and makes the collection accessible to the public.
